client: I've been really dreading something that's coming up next month — there's a family reunion, and honestly, I've been losing sleep over it. My cousin always finds a way to bring up my career in front of everyone and basically tears my choices apart, like I'm some kind of cautionary tale. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because the reunion is still going to happen either way.
therapist: It makes complete sense that you're losing sleep over this — anticipating that kind of public criticism from someone who's supposed to be family is genuinely painful, and your dread is a very understandable response to a real pattern you've experienced. I also hear that part of you feels a little hopeless about talking it through, like nothing can change the outcome, and I want to gently hold space for both of those feelings. Even if we can't cancel the reunion, I'm curious — when you imagine yourself *there* in that moment with your cousin, what feels like the most overwhelming part of it for you?

client: I think the most overwhelming part is just... not knowing when it's going to happen. Like, I can handle things when I can prepare for them, but with my cousin it's always this sudden comment out of nowhere, and then everyone's watching to see how I react. And then I freeze up and say nothing, which makes me feel even worse afterward because it's like I just let it happen again.
therapist: That freeze response makes so much sense — when we're caught off guard and feel like we're "on stage," our brain often goes into a kind of protective shutdown, and then the guilt afterward can feel almost worse than the comment itself. What I'm noticing is that there are actually two separate things causing you distress: the unpredictability of *when* it'll happen, and then the feeling of being stuck when it does. I'm wondering — if you knew with certainty that a comment was coming at some point during the reunion, do you think having even a simple, pre-prepared response in your back pocket might help that freeze feel a little less inevitable?

client: I mean, maybe... but honestly, even when I've tried to think of something to say ahead of time, my mind just goes completely blank in the moment anyway. It's like I know the words exist somewhere, but when my aunt or whoever makes that comment about me still being single, it's like my brain just... disconnects. And then I spend the whole drive home replaying it, thinking of all the things I should have said, which almost makes it worse.
therapist: That "disconnecting" feeling you're describing is so common under social stress — your nervous system is essentially hitting an alarm button, and it temporarily overrides the part of your brain where all those prepared responses are stored, which is why the words vanish even when you *know* they're there. And then that drive home becomes its own kind of punishment, where you're replaying and judging yourself on top of an already exhausting experience. I'm curious — when you're in that replay on the drive home, what's the harshest thing you tend to say to yourself about how you handled it?

client: Probably something like... "Why can't you just be normal?" or "Everyone else manages to hold a conversation, what's wrong with you?" It's like I become my own worst critic the second I'm alone in that car, and honestly it feels almost automatic at this point, like I don't even choose to do it. The worst part is I actually believe those things when I'm saying them to myself, even though I'd never say that to someone else going through the same thing.
therapist: What you just noticed at the end there is really profound — that you'd never speak to a friend the way you speak to yourself in that car, and yet somehow your own mind gets a free pass to be brutal with you. Those thoughts feeling "automatic" is actually a really important insight, because it means they're not facts or truth, they're just very well-worn mental habits that have been reinforced over time. I'm wondering — if a close friend called you after a family reunion and said "I froze when my cousin criticized me and now I can't stop thinking something is wrong with me," what would you actually say to them?

client: I'd probably tell them that freezing is a totally normal reaction, and that one awkward moment doesn't mean something is fundamentally broken about them. I'd remind them that their cousin was being unfair, not them. But... I don't know, it feels different when it's me saying it to myself — like I can see the logic when it's someone else, but when it's my own situation, my brain just doesn't buy it the same way.
therapist: You've just identified something really important — that you *have* the compassionate, logical voice inside you, it's just that your brain has a kind of "exception clause" that blocks it from applying to yourself, which is incredibly common but also worth gently challenging. That gap between what you'd offer a friend and what you allow yourself to receive isn't a sign that the logic is wrong — it actually suggests the harsh self-talk is working really hard to protect some deeper belief about yourself that feels very personal. I'm curious — when you hear yourself say "something is fundamentally broken about me," does any part of you have a sense of where that belief might have started, maybe long before your cousin ever made a comment at a reunion?

client: I go quiet for a moment because that question hits somewhere deeper than I expected. There's this image that comes up almost immediately — being a kid and feeling like I was always just slightly out of step with everyone else, like at family gatherings I'd say something and people would kind of look at me funny, and I'd spend the rest of the night replaying it. I think I learned pretty early that being "too much" or "too weird" was a problem, and somewhere along the way that turned into believing the problem was me, not just the moment.
therapist: Thank you for trusting me with that — what you just described is really significant, because it sounds like a much younger version of you drew a very understandable but painful conclusion: that the discomfort in the room was *your fault*, rather than just a moment of mismatch or misunderstanding. That little kid was doing their best to make sense of a confusing experience, and the belief they formed — "I am the problem" — has been quietly running in the background ever since, showing up in that car on the drive home all these years later. I'm wondering — when you picture that younger version of you at those family gatherings, feeling out of step and replaying moments alone, what do you feel toward them?

client: When I picture that kid... honestly, I feel sad for them. Like, they were just trying so hard to fit in and figure out what they did wrong, and there wasn't even really anything wrong to find. But I also feel kind of frustrated, because part of me wants to say "just get over it, stop being so sensitive" — which I guess is kind of what I still say to myself now.
therapist: That tension you're holding — sadness for that child alongside frustration with them — is so honest, and it's worth noticing that the voice telling them to "just get over it" sounds a lot like the same voice in the car on the drive home, which suggests it's been with you for a very long time. The sad part of you seems to already know the truth: that child wasn't too sensitive, they were just in an environment that didn't know how to make room for them. I'm curious — if the sad part of you could say just one thing directly to that younger version of you, what do you think it would want them to hear?

client: I sat with that for a second and... I think the sad part of me would want that kid to hear "you're not too much, you were just in the wrong place." But even saying that out loud feels weird, like I'm making excuses for myself or being self-indulgent. I guess I still can't fully shake the feeling that maybe they were right, that I really did need to toughen up.
therapist: What strikes me is that you just offered that child something genuinely healing — "you were in the wrong place" — and then almost immediately your mind moved to punish you for it, calling it self-indulgent, which is that same old protective voice rushing in to make sure you don't get "too comfortable" with self-compassion. It's worth gently questioning that voice: toughening up might have helped you survive those early experiences, but it also seems to be the thing that's keeping you up at night before a family reunion decades later, so maybe it's not protecting you as much as it once felt like it was. I'm wondering — what do you think "toughening up" actually cost that kid, and what might it still be costing you now?

client: That question kind of stops me in my tracks, honestly. I think it cost that kid the ability to just... let someone help him, or even admit he needed help, because showing that felt dangerous somehow. And yeah, I can see how that's still costing me now — I'm sitting here dreading a family reunion partly because I still don't know how to just be in a room with people without bracing for something to go wrong.
therapist: What you just said takes real courage to recognize — that the very armor that kept you safe as a kid has quietly become the thing that makes every room feel like something to brace against, rather than something to simply be in. And there's something quietly significant about the fact that you *are* here, talking about this, letting someone in a little — because that's actually the opposite of what that old protective pattern would have you do. I'm wondering — what does it feel like, right now in this moment, to have said all of that out loud?

client: Honestly? It feels a little strange, like I've just taken off a coat I've been wearing so long I forgot it wasn't part of me. There's something almost uncomfortable about it, like I'm waiting for something bad to happen because I let my guard down. I don't know if that makes sense, but sitting here saying all of this out loud makes me feel kind of... exposed, I guess.
therapist: That makes complete sense, and I want you to notice something: you just let your guard down, and nothing bad happened — you weren't judged, you weren't too much, and the room didn't turn against you, which is actually a small but real piece of evidence that quietly contradicts that old belief you formed as a kid. That feeling of exposure is what vulnerability feels like when you're not used to it, and it can genuinely feel like danger even when you're actually safe. I'm curious — sitting with that uncomfortable but honest feeling right now, is there any part of you, even a small one, that also feels something like relief?
